objections.claim: The stated problem is "the pre-check re-feeds issues a recent drain already declined and that nobody has touched since." The runner already knows which ids it fed at each tick and when (Appendix A step 4 adds exactly this logging). A runner-side record of `fed_ids @ timestamp`, cleared by the daily full drain, reproduces the filter's semantics (`changed_at` vs last-considered time, bounded window, full-drain backstop) with no faff command, no schema field, no beep-boop prose, and no cross-repo contract. The spec's rejection of runner-only designs ("duplicates ledger semantics in another repository") answers a jq-over-ledgers design, not a fed-log — the fed-log reads nothing of faff's ledger and duplicates no semantics. The DONE item "a drain leaves a `declined` record" is a restatement of the chosen mechanism, not an independent requirement derived from WHY.
objections.evidence: `### Design decisions` ("Where the fix lives"), `## 5. DESIGN DECISION RATIONALE` ("Where should the fix live?"), Appendix A step 4.
objections.predicted_consequence: The spec ships a new CLI verb, a closed-schema field, a writer-inventory entry, and prose edits in two beep-boop sites to carry a signal the runner could hold in one file on the volume it already owns; the first runner-side need that doesn't fit the ledger shape (e.g. per-label suppression) forces either another schema field or a runner-side shadow mechanism anyway.
objections.disposition_rationale: A runner fed-log suppresses issues a drain never reached (timeout, budget, sentry abort); only the drain knows what it declined. Added to section 5.

objections.claim: Step 3 makes any single unreadable or start-less ledger in the window keep **all** candidates. The WHY section establishes a tick cadence of a drain every ~5 minutes (~288 run dirs/day on this box alone), all inside the default 24-hour window. So one corrupt `run-ledger.json` among hundreds silently disables the entire cost saving — the design's sole purpose — with only a `degraded` string as a signal, and Appendix A's runner logs suppressed ids, not degraded causes. Skipping the unreadable run (treating it as carrying no declines) is equally fail-open: worst case it keeps candidates that run would have suppressed, which is today's behaviour for that run only, while the other ~287 ledgers keep filtering.
objections.evidence: `### 4.2 faff drain-filter` step 3; `## 1. WHY` (12 drains in one hour); `### Design principles` ("Fail open").
objections.predicted_consequence: A single truncated ledger (a crashed write — the same crash mode 4.5 already contemplates for `owner.status: running`) suppresses nothing for up to 24 hours, and the failure surfaces only if someone reads `degraded` in the runner's JSON output, which Appendix A never asks the runner to log or alert on.
objections.disposition_rationale: An unreadable ledger is skipped and keeps only candidates whose deciding run is older than it (4.2 step 4a2).

objections.claim: Step 4a2 keeps a candidate whenever an unreadable run is newer than the deciding run "**or its start is unknown**", and step 2's window exclusion can only skip runs whose start it can determine. A run directory whose ledger is malformed *and* whose name does not parse as `run-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS-*` (and whose `owner.started_at` is unreadable — exactly what a truncated/corrupt ledger plausibly loses) is therefore treated as newer than every deciding run, forever: it is never aged out by `--max-age-hours`, so from the tick it appears until someone deletes the directory, every candidate it could shadow is kept and the filter silently degrades to a no-op for those issues. The `degraded` list also grows by that run id on every invocation, forever.
objections.evidence: §4.2 steps 2, 3 and 4a2; the fail-open principle makes "keep" the forced outcome, but the spec never bounds how long an undatable unreadable run keeps forcing it.
objections.predicted_consequence: one corrupt run dir (e.g. a killed write during the very crashes the spec's own edge cases contemplate) permanently restores today's spend for the affected issues, with no signal stronger than a repeated `degraded` entry.
objections.disposition_rationale: Runs with no name time or started_at fall back to the dir mtime, so every run ages out.

As written, the spec builds a general suppression layer whose largest consumer is an inclusion bug.

objections.claim: The design's entire value proposition is that the runner calls `faff drain-filter` "with no model call" (§WHY, Appendix A step 2). But the supplied context establishes the opposite precondition: faff exists only inside the cage, and the only documented way faff gets installed there is `entrypoint.sh` — a script whose purpose is launching a model session. Appendix A asserts the sequence "run in the cage image … after `claude plugin update faff@faff`. No model call is involved" without establishing any mechanism by which the cage executes a bare command. The Assumptions section's validation is only "check that the runner ticket exists and is linked" — it never checks feasibility. Meanwhile the §5 rationale rejected the runner-side jq alternative on maintainability grounds, not cost grounds, so if the cage cannot host a command-mode entry, the chosen design loses to the rejected alternative on the one axis that justifies it (cheapness), and the faff half ships as dead weight.

objections.predicted_consequence: The runner ticket discovers the cage can only be entered via a model session; either each tick's pre-check now costs a session (worse than the incident), or the fallback fires every tick, the saving never lands, and FAFF-1412 closes with its faff half unused until someone re-opens the design.
objections.disposition_rationale: Appendix A gives the --entrypoint mechanism, a one-off feasibility check, and the outer-container fallback; failure-mode row added.

objections.claim: The suppression rule keeps a candidate only when `changed_at > declined.at`. The spec stamps `at` at CLI write time, but the drain may have *read* the tracker earlier in the run. A tracker change (human comment, label edit) that lands between the drain's read of the issue and the drain's `record-declined` write produces `declined.at` **later** than the true change time, so the very change that should re-eligible the issue suppresses it until the record expires. The spec's own anti-pattern reasoning — "the run's start time precedes any tracker write the run made, so suppressing on it could hide a human change made during the run" — is applied to reject `outcomes`-based suppression (step 4d) but the identical flaw is retained for the `declined` record, which is the path that actually ships. This is a trust decision the spec makes on the strength of an input (`at`) without establishing that it postdates the observation the suppression is based on.
objections.evidence: §4.1 ("`at: now`", "stamped by the CLI at write time, never by the caller"); §4.2 step 4c; the second anti-pattern bullet in §4.2, whose stated rationale condemns exactly this ordering but is not carried over to the chosen design; §4.5 clock-skew edge case covers `changed_at` skew only, not this direction.
objections.predicted_consequence: a human unblocks an issue while a drain is in flight; the drain's decline record postdates the change; every cheap tick suppresses the issue for up to `--max-age-hours` (24h default) despite the change — silently, with the runner log showing only `suppressed (declined, unchanged)`.
objections.disposition_rationale: at is the drain's observation time (--observed-at), recorded_at is the write time; a change between read and write keeps the issue.

objections.claim: §4.1 makes `record-declined` exit 2 when `--observed-at` is more than 60 seconds after now, but §4.3 instructs beep-boop to capture `observed_at` "immediately before the at-assembly tracker read of each candidate" and pass that same value to the decline write. The gap between a candidate's claim-before-admit re-read and its routed-out/claimed-by-peer disposition is whatever the drain does in between for that candidate (bundle-recover attempts, custody checks, admissibility evaluation) — not bounded by 60 seconds by anything in the spec. The validation rule and the call site's data flow are inconsistent as written.
objections.evidence: §4.1 "`--observed-at` must parse as ISO-8601 and must not be more than 60 seconds after now, else exit 2" vs §4.3 "capture `observed_at=$(date -u +%FT%TZ)` immediately before the at-assembly tracker read of each candidate … and pass it as `--observed-at` to every `record-declined` call for that candidate."

objections.disposition_rationale: The 60 s rule rejects only future times; any past observation is accepted. Wording clarified.

objections.claim: `--reason` is free text derived from drain dispositions (e.g. `claimed-by-peer:<cause>`, where `<cause>` can echo text from a refused bundle-recover or an inadmissibility message that quotes issue content). The spec sanitises it by trimming, collapsing newlines and capping length — but carriage returns and other control characters are not covered. Appendix A step 4 requires the runner to log the reason verbatim (`suppressed … (run-...: inadmissible:...)`), so a reason containing `\r` can forge or overwrite log lines in the runner's tick log, laundering attacker-influenced text into operator-facing infrastructure logs.
objections.evidence: §4.1 "`--reason` is trimmed and has newlines collapsed to spaces; empty, or longer than 200 characters after that, is exit 2"; Appendix A step 4 logs the reason; DeclineRecord `reason` examples in §3.
objections.predicted_consequence: forged/spoofed lines in the runner's pre-check log, attributed to the filter, crafted from content the drain read (issue titles, bundle-recover diagnostics).
objections.disposition_rationale: All control characters in --reason replaced by spaces; test added.

objections.claim: The saving depends entirely on the runner invoking `faff drain-filter --runs-dir /home/faff/state/runs`, but neither the spec nor the supplied context establishes that the run directories actually live at that on-volume path. The explore notes say only that the state volume is mounted at `/home/faff/state` and that the runs dir is "symlinked to `/home/faff/app/.faff/runs`" — the direction and the on-volume location of the real directories are never pinned. Because the filter fails open with `degraded: "no-runs-dir"` and exit 0, a wrong path is indistinguishable from a quiet day: the Appendix A step-2 check ("the command must print a `FilterResult` and start no model session") passes verbatim against a wrong path, since an all-kept result with `degraded` set is still a well-formed `FilterResult`. The spec's own fail-open principle, correct inside the cage, here silences the one check that exists to validate the deployment.
objections.evidence: Appendix A steps 2 and 4; `explore.md` ("State volume faff-state mounted in the cage at /home/faff/state; runs dir symlinked to /home/faff/app/.faff/runs"); spec §4.2 step 1 (`Missing runs_dir -> keep all, degraded "no-runs-dir", exit 0`).
objections.predicted_consequence: The runner ticket ships, the check passes, the incident's cost loop continues unchanged, and the first signal is a human noticing `pre-check: … degraded no-runs-dir` in tick logs — or never, since step 4 logs degraded but nobody is required to alert on it.
objections.disposition_rationale: On-volume path pinned from drain.sh (ln -sfn /home/faff/state/runs ...); the one-off check requires degraded null; no-runs-dir logged as a deployment fault.

objections.claim: The spec states "Fail open" as a design principle but scopes it to the filter ("Any doubt … keeps the candidate"). The beep-boop call sites in 4.3 are instructed to run `record-declined` after each disposition with no tolerance clause for its failure modes. `record-declined` has a real failure path the spec itself defines — exit 3 on "the locked write failed" — and two drains can plausibly contend for the same run's lock (the incident shows drains firing every few minutes; a long drain overlaps the next tick's targeted pass only if the targeted pass is what drains, but the daily full drain and a targeted drain can overlap). If beep-boop treats the non-zero exit as a step failure, the drain aborts after the disposition but before later candidates — the writer becomes a gate, the exact inversion of the stated principle.
objections.evidence: "### Design principles — **Fail open.** This is a cost filter, never a gate on work" (scoped to the filter); "### Commands — `record-declined` … 3 no run dir … or the locked write failed"; "### 4.3 beep-boop prose — after recording the `routed-out` outcome, run `record-declined`".
objections.predicted_consequence: a lock contention or missing run dir on one candidate ends the drain early; the remaining candidates are never considered and never get decline records, so the loop the spec exists to stop keeps burning tokens — and the failure is invisible unless someone reads the drain log.
objections.disposition_rationale: A failed record-declined is logged and never stops the drain (4.3, DONE).

objections.claim: The decline record is the first faff artifact whose effect outlives the run and gates a *future* actor (the runner pre-check). The spec explicitly decouples the writer from evidence of consideration: 4.1 says the command "does not require the issue to be in `admitted`", and nothing requires the issue to appear in the run's `outcomes`, candidates, or events at all. The writer is invoked by the beep-boop agent, which reads untrusted issue content; a hostile issue description (or simply a buggy drain) can therefore call `record-declined --issue <any-other-id>` and suppress issues the run never looked at, for every tick in the window. The spec establishes who writes the record but not that the record attests to a decision this run actually made.
objections.evidence: §4.1 "It does not require the issue to be in `admitted`."; §3 Decline record definition; §4.3 call sites; the threat checklist's "when the spec grants authority on the strength of an input, the spec must establish who can write that input" — here the input (`--issue`) is agent-chosen with no binding to run contents.
objections.predicted_consequence: A drain steered by issue content (or a defect) suppresses unrelated issues from the cheap pass for up to `--max-age-hours` (24h default); work is delayed, not lost — the daily full drain and the fail-open design cap the damage, which is why this is not major.
objections.disposition_rationale: Effect is a delay of at most max-age on the cheap pass, never lost work; the ledger is already agent-writable under a shared uid, so binding would not stop a forger. Failure-mode row added.

objections.claim: The spec mandates exit 2 when "a flag is unknown or invalid", but never defines what makes `--max-age-hours` or `--now` invalid (negative? zero? non-numeric? unparseable `--now`?). A build that accepts `--max-age-hours -1` (window empty, everything kept — fail-open) and a build that exits 2 both satisfy the text.
objections.evidence: `### Commands` exit-code line: "2 when stdin is not a JSON array of objects, or a flag is unknown or invalid"; contrast `--issue`/`--reason`/`--observed-at`, whose validity rules are spelled out in 4.1.
objections.predicted_consequence: The DONE item "exits 2 on non-array stdin or an unknown flag" can be decided, but the exit-code behaviour for a malformed `--max-age-hours` cannot be verified either way; two conforming builds disagree and no test in §7 can arbitrate.
objections.disposition_rationale: --max-age-hours 1..168 and --now ISO validity defined; tests added.
